title: God is simple (ST I.3)
hook: God has no parts; his being and his essence are one

segments.voice: Yesterday, the fourth and fifth ways: degrees of goodness, and an arrow that doesn't aim. Your line was arguments invite, not force. Where did you give your reasons and stop pushing? Day one thousand one hundred fifty-nine.

A kid with a screwdriver has the back off an old radio on the kitchen floor. Screws in a saucer. A circuit board. A speaker cone. Wires in four colors. He's learning what grown-ups know: open almost anything and you find pieces. A sandwich is pieces. A song is notes. A sentence is words. You are a body and a breath, habits and moods, a past and a plan. Things are put together. So here's the question Thomas Aquinas asks next, right after the five ways: if God is, what is God made of? His answer is today's word.
screen: `A RADIO ON THE KITCHEN FLOOR.` → `OPEN IT: PIECES.` → `WHAT IS GOD MADE OF?`

segments.voice: Thomas opens with a confession. We can't know what God is, he says, only what God is not. So he works by taking things away. First, a body. God is not one. He leans on Jesus's words in John, in the Douay-Rheims: "God is a spirit." Then he goes further than you might expect. God isn't made of anything at all. No stuff plus shape. No pieces. And no add-ons either. Here's what he means. You have a good habit, maybe patience. But you are not your patience. You could lose it on a bad Monday and still be you. There's a gap between who you are and what you have. In God, Thomas says, there's no gap. God doesn't have goodness the way you have patience. And then the deepest step. For everything else, what it is and that it is are two different things. You can know what a unicorn is without it existing. Your being is lent. In God, Thomas says, the two are one: what God is, is to be. Why care? Because, Thomas argues, anything made of parts depends on its parts, and on whatever put them together. A God built of pieces would need a builder. The first cause of the five ways can't be like that. That's the meaning of the word. Simplicity here doesn't mean plain, or easy to understand. Thomas reaches it the hard way, by saying what God is not. It means whole. Undivided. Nothing in God pulling against anything else in God. Some readers find that strange and cold at first. Others find it a rest. On Thomas's account, a God with no parts is a God who can't come apart.
screen: `WE KNOW WHAT GOD IS NOT.` · `NO BODY, NO PIECES, NO ADD-ONS.` · `WHAT GOD IS, IS TO BE.` · `PARTS WOULD NEED A BUILDER.` · then, large: `GOD IS A SPIRIT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: sit with one simple thing. Settle, and breathe. Choose one thing and only one. A single breath, in and out. A candle flame. A smooth stone in your palm. The sound of the room. Let everything else fall to the edges. When your mind starts taking the thing apart, naming, comparing, planning, come back to the one thing, whole. Don't analyze it. Just let it be one. If you pray, you can rest there before the God Thomas calls simple. If you don't, just stay with the one thing until the bell. The bell holds the time.
Simplicity. In Thomas Aquinas, not plainness but wholeness: God has no parts, and in God what God is and that God is are one. Today's word.
Your line: no parts. Today, when you feel pulled in several directions at once, stop for one breath and do just one thing, whole. Day one thousand one hundred fifty-nine.

howItsDone: Catholic theology teaches divine simplicity as part of the doctrine of God, and readers of the Summa meet it right after the five ways, in the Summa's third question.

pairs: something you have, and can lose

myth: for Thomas, 'simple' means God is easy to understand
it means not made of parts; Thomas says we grasp it by saying what God is not.
Thomas says that in God, what God is and that God is are one
for everything else they are two; God's being is not lent.
Thomas says God has goodness the way a person has a good habit
a person can gain or lose a habit; in God, Thomas says, there's no gap between who God is and what God has.

fork.setup: a child asks Thomas: what is God made of? which is closest to his answer?
options: the finest, lightest stuff there is.
nothing: God isn't made of parts at all.
fork.reveal: Thomas says God has no body, no stuff plus shape, no add-ons: anything made of parts would depend on them and need a builder.

original.note: Latin: simplicity, being uncomposed — Thomas's word for God having no parts.

trapdoor: what you thought: God is simple, so faith should be easy.
what it means: God isn't built from parts; there's no gap between who God is and what God has.
what a scholar hears: no body, no matter and form, no accidents; essence and existence one in God; reached by saying what God is not.

sources.ref: Summa Theologiae I, q. 3 (prologue and articles 1–7)

notes: ST I.3 paraphrased: prologue (we cannot know what God is, but rather what he is not); a.1 not a body (sed contra John 4:24); a.2 no matter and form; a.3 God is his own essence; a.4 essence and existence the same in God; a.6 no accidents; a.7 altogether simple, since every composite depends on its parts and has a cause. Confirm.
The patience example and the unicorn are the script's illustrations of accidents and of essence versus existence; confirm they are fair.
'Some readers find that strange and cold at first. Others find it a rest.' is offered as a range of responses, not a claim about how many.
Douay-Rheims John 4:24: confirm wording ('God is a spirit').
Editor: cut 'Thomas is clear that it's the opposite' (overstated); framed 'a God who can't come apart' as Thomas's account, not the narrator's; howItsDone no longer claims what students usually do.
